questions.description: A September 19 that nobody in Mexico City wants to live through again.
questions.question: Every September 19, Mexico holds a nationwide drill in memory of a big 20th-century earthquake. What year was it?
hints: It struck on a Thursday morning, just after seven o'clock.
It happened a year before Mexico hosted its second World Cup.
It was during Miguel de la Madrid's presidency.
questions.fun_fact: After the quake, the famous “Topos” (Moles) were born: rescue volunteers who now help in disasters all over the world.

media.author: Mina Noei

questions.description: A lizard that looks like a mini dinosaur and eats ants for breakfast, lunch and dinner.
questions.question: In Mexico it's called the camaleón cornudo; it lives in the desert and eats ants. Why does it squirt blood from its eyes?
questions.answer: To scare off coyotes and foxes
wrong_answers: To cool off in the sun
hints: It raises the blood pressure in its head so much that tiny vessels near its eyes burst.
The blood tastes awful to certain animals.
It works best on the dog's wild relatives.
questions.fun_fact: The camaleón cornudo isn't a chameleon at all: it's a horned lizard, and its squirt of blood can reach more than 1 m (3 ft).

media.author: Room237

questions.description: The tastiest nighttime alarm clock in Mexico's neighborhoods.
questions.question: It's nighttime, and a bit of the famous recording plays down the street: “¡Ricos… oaxaqueños, calientitos!” Who is passing by?
hints: What he sells is a favorite for dinner or breakfast.
He often brings atole or champurrado too.
He sells something wrapped in banana leaf or corn husk and steamed.
questions.fun_fact: On February 2, Candelaria Day, whoever found the little figurine in the rosca has to treat everyone to tamales.

media.credit: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net). · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Photograph by Mike Peel (www.mikepeel.net).

questions.description: The only place where you're allowed to melt with happiness.
questions.question: Look at the photo: in Mexico, at which shop do you buy this?
hints: It's very cold inside its freezers.
It tastes best on a hot day.
Many of these shops are called “La Michoacana.”
questions.fun_fact: Many paleterías are called “La Michoacana” because the business spread from Tocumbo, a small town in Michoacán.

media.author: P1898

hints: You order it with your torta or your tacos.
It has bubbles and comes in a bottle or a can.
It's a short way of saying “refresco.”
questions.fun_fact: Mexico is one of the countries where people drink the most soda per person in the world.

questions.description: At the corner stand, a glass barrel holds the best cure for the afternoon heat.
questions.question: Look at the photo: which agua fresca is it?
hints: It's white like milk.
It has cinnamon on top.
It's made with rice.
questions.fun_fact: Mexican horchata is made with rice, but in Valencia, Spain, it's made with tiger nuts, a tiny tuber.

media.author: Sharon Hahn Darlin

questions.description: A meat that takes a long, hot bath before it lands in your taco.
questions.question: They cook for hours in a big copper pot, in their own lard, until golden and tender. Which animal do carnitas come from?
hints: It's a farm animal.
Chicharrón and cueritos come from the same animal.
It goes “oink, oink.”
questions.fun_fact: The most famous carnitas in Mexico come from Michoacán, especially from the town of Quiroga.

questions.description: The only spot in the house where a cow, three kings and an angel live together without fighting.
questions.question: In December you set it up at home with moss, hay and little figures of Joseph, Mary and the shepherds, and on the 24th the Baby Jesus is laid in it. What is it?
wrong_answers: The Day of the Dead altar
hints: It stays up until Día de la Candelaria (Candlemas).
It has a little stable, animals and even the Three Kings.
Its name comes from a word that means being born.
questions.fun_fact: Many Mexican nativity scenes have figures that aren't in the Bible, like a little devil, a rooster or even a woman making tortillas.

media.author: Thayne Tuason

questions.description: A gift deliverer who shows up without GPS and still finds your shoe.
questions.question: I arrive on the night of January 5. In Mexico they say I come on horseback, I'm the one with the white beard, and I brought gold to Baby Jesus. Who am I?
hints: I'm one of the Three Kings.
They say I'm the oldest of the three.
My name starts with M.
questions.fun_fact: In the Mexican version, Gaspar arrives on a camel and Baltasar on an elephant, which is why many nativity scenes include a little elephant.

questions.question: The National Silver Fair awards prizes to jewelry like this. Who revived silversmithing in its host city in the 1930s?
hints: He wasn't born in Mexico.
He was an architect and a teacher in New Orleans.
He opened a workshop in 1931 and trained hundreds of silversmiths.
questions.fun_fact: Before coming to Mexico, Spratling shared an apartment in New Orleans with the writer William Faulkner.

media.credit: Calipso03 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Calipso03

questions.description: A cousin of flan that stayed in the oven a little too long.
questions.question: This jericalla, a dessert of milk, egg and cinnamon with a toasted top, is typical of one city. Which one?
hints: It's a city in western Mexico.
It's said to have been born at the Hospicio Cabañas, to feed the children there.
It's the home of mariachi and the torta ahogada.
questions.fun_fact: One legend says its name comes from Jérica, the town in Spain where its inventor came from.

questions.description: A town so quiet that even the whispers have an echo.
questions.question: I own the Media Luna ranch and rule over Comala. My son comes looking for me and finds only whispers. Who am I?
hints: I'm a character in a 1955 novel.
Juan Rulfo wrote me.
My name is also the title of the book.
questions.fun_fact: Gabriel García Márquez said he had read “Pedro Páramo” so many times he could recite it from memory.

media.credit: Yaomautzin Ohtokani Olvera Lara · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yaomautzin Ohtokani Olvera Lara

questions.description: A parade where the skeletons dance better than your uncles at a wedding.
questions.question: Since when has Mexico City held its big Day of the Dead parade?
hints: It's much newer than it looks.
It was inspired by a movie.
That movie is a James Bond film released in 2015.
questions.fun_fact: The James Bond movie “Spectre” opens with a Day of the Dead parade that didn't exist yet; after seeing it, Mexico City created a real one.

media.author: Aline Livier

questions.description: The only castle in the Americas with an emperor, cadets and a line for the museum.
questions.question: The Niños Héroes fought at this castle in 1847. In which park in Mexico City is it?
hints: Emperor Maximilian and Carlota lived there.
It's the city's most famous park, and it has a zoo.
Its name in Nahuatl means “grasshopper hill.”
questions.fun_fact: It's the only castle in the Americas where an emperor lived, and today it's the National Museum of History.

media.author: Own work

questions.description: He came from Europe with a crown, a cape and big plans to rule… and things didn't go as planned.
questions.question: I was an Archduke of Austria. The French army brought me to rule Mexico in 1864, and my empire ended in Querétaro in 1867. Who am I?
hints: I wasn't born in the Americas.
My wife's name was Carlota.
I was the emperor of the Second Mexican Empire.
questions.fun_fact: Maximilian had the Paseo de la Emperatriz laid out, and today it is Mexico City's Paseo de la Reforma.

media.credit: Guillermo Ruiz · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Guillermo Ruiz

questions.description: Your face turned into a patriotic canvas, glitter included.
questions.question: In September you paint the Mexican flag on your cheek, starting with green. Which color comes after white?
hints: It's a color on the flag.
You already used green at the start.
It's the color of a ripe tomato.
questions.fun_fact: The green, white and red come from the flag of the Army of the Three Guarantees in 1821.

media.author: ajay_suresh

questions.question: Lots of students do gymnastics moves at the same time to music, and show it off in the November 20 parade. What is it called?
hints: The students don't play any instruments.
Sometimes they use hoops, balls or ribbons.
Its name has a word that has to do with the beat of the music.
questions.fun_fact: The November 20 parade is also called the sports parade because of all the athletes and gymnasts who march in it.

questions.description: The song that even the most off-key singer belts out at full volume.
questions.question: “Cielito lindo” is sung at patriotic fiestas and in stadiums, and its chorus starts “Ay, ay, ay, ay…”. What comes next?
questions.answer: Canta y no llores (sing and don't cry)
wrong_answers: Baila y no pares (dance and don't stop)
Ríe y no grites (laugh and don't shout)
Vuelve y no te vayas (come back and don't go)
hints: It's advice to stay cheerful.
It has to do with using your voice.
Doing the opposite of what it says would mean bursting into tears.
questions.fun_fact: “Cielito lindo” was written by Quirino Mendoza y Cortés around 1882.

questions.description: Before shopping malls, neighbors grouped together by trade.
questions.question: I'm a pedestrian street in Mexico City's Historic Center. In colonial times I was called “Plateros” because the silversmiths' guild worked there. Who am I?
hints: I run from the Zócalo toward the Torre Latinoamericana.
My name was changed in 1914.
Today I carry the surname of the president who started the Revolution.
questions.fun_fact: In 1914, Pancho Villa himself put up the plaque with the street's new name.

media.author: W.carter

questions.description: Words that arrived before Cortés and decided to stay for good.
questions.question: Which of these words for places does NOT come from Nahuatl?
hints: Three of them were used in the Valley of Mexico.
The odd one out comes from another Indigenous language, spoken far from the Valley of Mexico.
It comes from a language of the Yucatán Peninsula.
questions.fun_fact: “Tianguis” comes from the Nahuatl “tianquiztli”, which means market.

hints: It is one of five Franciscan missions that are World Heritage Sites.
The town where it stands bears the friar's surname.
The capital of that state has a famous aqueduct.
questions.fun_fact: The mission's town is called Jalpan de Serra in honor of the friar, who was born on the island of Mallorca.

questions.question: At a market in Oaxaca, you try on an embroidered blouse made of manta. What fiber is manta made of?

The plant grows fluffy white puffs.
Most T-shirts are made of the same fiber.
questions.fun_fact: Manta is unbleached cotton cloth, which is why it has that typical off-white color.

hints: You have to handle them very carefully.
They shine brightly and light passes through them.
They're shaped by blowing, and if they fall on the floor they shatter.
questions.fun_fact: In Chignahuapan the ornaments are painted by hand, and many carry whatever name the customer asks for.

It's the capital of Jalisco.

There's something inside it.
It holds oats or corn.

It's held on Plaza San Jacinto.
It's home to the house-studio of Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo.
questions.fun_fact: While the bazaar fills an old mansion, painters show their canvases outside on the plaza.

Its sweet sap, before it ferments, is called aguamiel.
It's a close relative of the agave used for tequila.
questions.fun_fact: Before the Spanish arrived, pulque was a sacred drink that almost only elders, priests and people at ceremonies were allowed to drink.

Families bring cempasúchil flowers.

This leader had started the rebellion in a town in Guanajuato.

Its capital is Hermosillo.

media.author: David Ratledge

questions.description: Gown, high heels and nerves of steel: welcome to Hollywood's fanciest night.

media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: A traveler who crosses five states and never once asks for a ride.
questions.question: “I'm born in the State of Mexico, cross Querétaro, Guanajuato and Michoacán, and end in Lake Chapala.” Which river am I?
hints: I flow through the center of the country, not along a border.
After leaving Chapala I carry on under another name: the Santiago River.
I share my name with a city near Toluca.
questions.fun_fact: Together, the Lerma and the Santiago form one of the longest river systems in Mexico.

media.credit: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico

questions.description: A tianguis so big that not even the Sunday one in your neighborhood comes close.
questions.question: Hernán Cortés wrote that at the great market of Tlatelolco, on the shore of Lake Texcoco, about how many people gathered every day?
hints: It was the biggest market the Spaniards had ever seen.
It was more than the population of many Spanish cities at the time.
It's a five-digit number.
questions.fun_fact: At the Tlatelolco market, cacao beans were used as money.

media.credit: Luis Alvaz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Luis Alvaz

questions.description: A craft so devilishly good that even el chamuco shows off his portrait.
questions.question: The Purépecha women of Ocumicho, Michoacán, shape colorful little clay devils. According to one village tale, why did they start making them?
questions.answer: So the devil had a place to live and left the village alone
wrong_answers: To win a bet the devil had made with the village
To scare children who didn't obey their parents
To ask the devil to bring rain in the dry season
hints: It has to do with keeping a very mischievous someone calm.
They say the devil used to roam the village freely, playing tricks.
They gave el chamuco his own little clay house so he'd stop bothering people.
questions.fun_fact: Many Ocumicho devils show the devil in everyday scenes: driving, at the doctor's, or even playing soccer.

media.credit: Fernando Hernández Ramírez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Fernando Hernández Ramírez

questions.description: The tiniest real estate on the whole peninsula.
questions.question: In Yucatán, some farmers build a little stone house in the middle of their milpa. According to Maya tradition, what is it for?
questions.answer: For an alux to live in and guard the milpa
wrong_answers: To store next year's corn seeds
For souls to rest on Día de Muertos
To offer the first elote to the rain god
hints: Farmers often leave food and drink in the little house.
They believe it's for someone who lives in the milpa all year, not just for one day or season.
It's like a little Maya goblin that needs a home of its own.
questions.fun_fact: They say that if the alux gets no offerings, it turns mischievous: it throws pebbles and scares anyone passing through the milpa.

media.credit: KONTRA.PKC · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: KONTRA.PKC

questions.description: Deer have a lawyer too, and it doesn't charge in pesos.
questions.question: You're hunting in the Yucatán bush and kill more deer than you need. According to the Maya, who will punish you?
hints: It's a guardian of the animals of the wild.
Hunters feared it most, more than farmers did.
They say it looks like a little deer with a wasp nest between its antlers.
questions.fun_fact: Traditional Maya hunters asked it for permission and left it offerings before going out to hunt.

media.credit: USFWS Pacific · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: USFWS Pacific

questions.description: The longest-working model in all of Mexico, and she's never once asked for a raise.
questions.question: Since 1930, a mannequin in a wedding dress in a Chihuahua shop has looked so real that people say she's a person. What is her nickname?
hints: She stands in downtown Chihuahua City.
Her nickname comes from the name of the shop's owner.
It sounds like an affectionate nickname for “Pascuala.”
questions.fun_fact: Some people swear her eyes follow customers around and that her dress is changed behind closed doors.

media.credit: Jwslubbock · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jwslubbock

questions.description: A soup that shows up with its own little slice, ready for the photo.
questions.question: This is sopa de lima, a chicken broth with strips of fried tortilla. Which Mexican regional cuisine is it typical of?
hints: It's a cuisine from southeastern Mexico that uses lots of achiote and citrus.
Its region has coasts on both the Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of Mexico.
It's from the peninsula where Mérida and Chichén Itzá are.
questions.fun_fact: The Yucatán lima isn't just any lime: it has a very fragrant aroma and a taste unlike the common lime.

media.credit: Isaacvp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Isaacvp

questions.description: A paper so tough it survives centuries… and even your little brother with crayons.
questions.question: You’re at a crafts market looking at birds painted on amate paper. Before the Spanish Conquest, what was painted on this paper?
hints: They folded up like an accordion.
They held calendars, histories and lists of tributes.
They were the books of the peoples of Mesoamerica.
questions.fun_fact: Amate paper is made by boiling tree bark and beating the strips with a stone until they form a sheet.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: Black, sticky and not something you’d want to spread on your toast.
questions.question: Chapopote seeps out of the ground on the Gulf coast. It’s black and sticky, and today it’s used to waterproof roofs. What kind of substance is it?
hints: It forms underground over millions of years.
Veracruz and Tabasco are famous for this kind of wealth.
Pemex’s business is getting it out of the ground.
questions.fun_fact: Coastal peoples used chapopote as glue and to waterproof canoes long before refineries existed.

media.credit: Lldenke · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Lldenke

questions.description: Mexico’s oldest arm workout, and no monthly gym fee.
questions.question: It’s made of volcanic stone, has three legs and is used with a long stone called a metlapil or mano. What is a metate for?
hints: You use it on your knees, pushing forward.
It’s where the dough gets made.
Afterward, the tortillas are cooked on the comal.
questions.fun_fact: Grinding on a metate was so important that many families passed theirs down from grandmother to granddaughter.

media.credit: Hiart · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hiart

questions.description: A chile so proud of its hometown that it took the town's name.
questions.question: Look at this chile pepper: its name comes from a Mexican city. Which one?
hints: It's a plump green chile that's often eaten pickled.
The city is famous for its coffee and its drizzly weather.
Its name can be spelled with an X or a J.
questions.fun_fact: A chipotle is a ripe jalapeño that has been dried and smoked.

media.credit: Rob Holland from Decatur, GA, USA · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rob Holland from Decatur, GA, USA

questions.description: A giant with its arms up, as if it's been in a stick-up for 100 years.
questions.question: The saguaro grows over 12 m (40 ft) tall, sprouts arms after many years and grows only in one desert Mexico shares with the US. Which one?
hints: It's in northwestern Mexico.
It reaches the Gulf of California and Arizona.
It's named after the state whose capital is Hermosillo.
questions.fun_fact: A saguaro can take about 70 years to grow its first arm.

media.credit: Gentry George, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gentry George, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service

questions.description: A pumpkin that didn't want to be a lantern and chose to be delicious instead.
questions.question: Calabaza en tacha is cooked with piloncillo and cinnamon and eaten around Día de Muertos. What kind of food is it?
hints: It cooks slowly in a big pot.
The pumpkin pieces turn shiny and sticky.
It's served after the meal, with a glass of milk.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from the tachas, the big pans once used on Mexico's sugar haciendas.

media.credit: John Cummings · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Cummings

questions.description: The skinny, wild grandpa of the most famous corncob in the world.
questions.question: It's a wild Mexican grass with tiny ears of a few very hard kernels. About 9,000 years ago people domesticated it, and it became corn. What is it called?
hints: Its name comes from Nahuatl.
It was domesticated in the Balsas River valley.
Its name starts with “teo”, like Teotihuacan.
questions.fun_fact: An ear of teosinte has only about 10 kernels, each in a super-hard shell.

media.credit: Huntington and Page; · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: A shy god jumped into the fire, and that's how the light that gives us our suntan was switched on.
questions.question: If you want to visit the place where, according to the Mexica, the gods gathered to create the Fifth Sun, which archaeological site do you go to?
hints: The Mexica gave this abandoned city its name in Nahuatl.
It was already in ruins when the Mexica arrived.
It is near Mexico City and has the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon.
questions.fun_fact: Teotihuacan means something like “the place where men become gods.”

media.credit: Chitrapa · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Chitrapa

questions.description: A bone collector who never lends them to anyone… well, almost never.
questions.question: In my kingdom I keep the bones of the people of past suns. When a god came to ask for them, I gave him a conch with no holes to play. Who am I?
hints: My home is at the very bottom, on the last of nine levels.
I'm often shown as a skeleton, sometimes with owls and spiders nearby.
I'm the lord of the place of the dead, Mictlán.
questions.fun_fact: Quetzalcóatl managed to play the conch because some worms drilled holes in it and some bees made it sound.

media.credit: Didier Descouens · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Didier Descouens

questions.description: A Sunday broth that makes Monday hurt a little less.
questions.question: This consomé comes with barbacoa tacos. What animal is the traditional barbacoa of Hidalgo and central Mexico made from?
hints: It's a farm animal.
It grazes in flocks on the hills of Hidalgo.
Its babies are called lambs.
questions.fun_fact: The consomé is made from the juices the meat releases while it cooks wrapped in maguey leaves inside a pit in the ground.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: A meat so thin you could almost read through it.
questions.question: It's beef cut into very thin strips, salted and dried; in Oaxaca it's grilled over charcoal and goes on tlayudas. What is it called?
hints: It's sold in the smoke-filled aisle of the 20 de Noviembre market.
Before refrigerators, salting and drying meat was the way to keep it.
Its name starts with “ta.”
questions.fun_fact: At the 20 de Noviembre market in Oaxaca, you pick your raw meat and they grill it right there in an aisle full of smoke.

media.credit: Bluerasberry · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bluerasberry

questions.description: A tortilla that switched grains and moved far away from home.
questions.question: Flour tortillas are made from wheat, not corn. They're used for burritos and served with carne asada. Which part of Mexico are they typical of?
hints: It's very hot there, and there are deserts.
It's a land of big cattle ranches and cowboys.
Sonora and Chihuahua are there.
questions.fun_fact: In Sonora they make huge, paper-thin flour tortillas called “sobaqueras”.

media.credit: Vigilantcosmicpenguin · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vigilantcosmicpenguin

questions.description: A chile that got wrinkly with age but gained character.
questions.question: What dried chile, almost black with a chocolatey flavor, comes from a type of poblano and goes into mole poblano?
hints: It's one of the three classic chiles in mole poblano.
It's a cousin of the ancho chile, which is more reddish.
It's a poblano left to ripen until very dark before drying; the ancho comes from a redder one.
questions.fun_fact: Classic mole poblano uses three dried chiles: ancho, pasilla and mulato.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: Empanadas with the ocean hidden inside.
questions.question: These empanadas from the coasts of Sinaloa and Nayarit are filled with shrimp. Which group of animals do shrimp belong to?
hints: It has a hard shell.
It has lots of legs and antennae.
Crabs and lobsters belong to the same group.
questions.fun_fact: Shrimp turn pink when cooked because the heat releases a pigment called astaxanthin.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: A drink so old it has its own fair and even its own goddess.
questions.question: You're at the Feria del Pulque, and a mural shows the Mexica goddess of the maguey. Who is she?
hints: In the myth, the first maguey plant grew from her.
She was the mother of the Centzon Totochtin, the 400 rabbits of pulque.
Her name starts with “Maya…”.
questions.fun_fact: Before it ferments, the sweet sap taken from the maguey is called aguamiel (honey water).

media.credit: ArCaRa · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ArCaRa

questions.description: A parade so cheerful that even the puppets grow 3 meters tall to see it.
questions.question: In Oaxaca, before a saint's feast, a parade fills the streets with a band, giant cane “monos” and cloth globes called marmotas. What is it called?
hints: It usually goes out at night, among fireworks and lights.
Young women dance with decorated baskets on their heads.
Its name comes from the Latin “calendae”, the first day of the month.
questions.fun_fact: The marmota of a calenda is a big cloth ball on a pole that someone spins while dancing.

media.credit: User: (WT-shared) Anyludes at  wts wikivoyage · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: User: (WT-shared) Anyludes at  wts wikivoyage

questions.description: A fair named after a saint people pray to for the impossible, like finding a parking spot.
questions.question: Every May, the Feria de Santa Rita honors Saint Rita of Cascia, patron saint of a state capital in northern Mexico. Which one?
hints: It's in the north, surrounded by desert and mountains.
Miguel Hidalgo was executed by firing squad there in 1811.
It's the capital of the country's largest state.
questions.fun_fact: The feast of Saint Rita of Cascia is on May 22, which is why the fair falls in that month.

media.credit: blmcalifornia · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: blmcalifornia

questions.description: Your grandma thinks it's scarier than any horror movie.
questions.question: It's the cool damp of the night: laundry left out is wet by morning, and grandmas say never go out in it without a jacket. What is it called in Mexico?
hints: It only shows up after the sun has gone down.
It isn't rain: it falls without you seeing it.
Its name sounds like the English word for very calm.
questions.fun_fact: Long ago, “el sereno” was also the night watchman who walked the streets calling out the time.

media.credit: Dennis G. Jarvis · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dennis G. Jarvis

questions.description: A genre with more verses than the audience has patience for.
questions.question: It's a song that tells a story. It told of the deeds of Villa and Zapata, and “La Adelita” is a famous example. What is this genre called?
hints: It was sung from town to town to tell what was happening.
Today there are also norteño versions of this genre.
Its name comes from the Spanish verb for “to run.”
questions.fun_fact: During the Revolution, corridos worked like newscasts, bringing news of the battles to people who couldn't read.

media.credit: SMU Central University Libraries · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SMU Central University Libraries

questions.description: A furry neighbor who shows up at night when nobody invited him.
questions.question: The word “mapache” (raccoon) comes from Nahuatl. Roughly, what does it mean?
questions.answer: The one who grabs everything with its hands
wrong_answers: The one with the striped tail
The one who only comes out at night
The one who wears a black mask
hints: The name is about something the raccoon does, not about its color.
It seems to “wash” its food in water.
Its front paws look like little hands.
questions.fun_fact: A raccoon's front paws are so sensitive that it can recognize its food by touch, without looking at it.

media.credit: Rhododendrites · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rhododendrites

questions.description: A tree with a tongue-twister name and a reputation as a grandma's remedy.
questions.question: At a market herb stall, you buy cuachalalate for a traditional stomach tea. What part of the tree are you being sold?
hints: It's sold in hard, dry pieces.
It's an outer part taken off the tree.
It's what covers the trunk.
questions.fun_fact: Cuachalalate grows in the dry forests of western and southern Mexico.

media.credit: AlejandroLinaresGarcia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AlejandroLinaresGarcia

questions.description: Water in such a hurry to get down that it doesn't even say goodbye to the mountain.
questions.question: Look at the photo: these Chiapas waterfalls share their name with the draft of air that, grandmas say, gives you a stiff neck. What are they called?
hints: They're near Comitán, on the San Vicente River.
Their tallest drop is called the Velo de Novia (Bridal Veil).
The name sounds like a chiflido, a whistle.
questions.fun_fact: The Velo de Novia at El Chiflón falls from about 120 m (394 ft) high.

media.credit: User:Angel06x · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: User:Angel06x

questions.description: A forest that takes up more room on the map than a cousin asleep on the couch.
questions.question: It covers slopes along Mexico's Pacific side, from Sonora to Chiapas, and is the tropical vegetation that covers the most land in Mexico. What is it called?
hints: Its trees rarely grow taller than 15 m (49 ft).
In the dry season it looks gray and colorless.
Its name says it loses its leaves.
questions.fun_fact: The palo mulato (gumbo-limbo) is nicknamed the “tourist tree” because its red bark peels like sunburned skin.

media.credit: Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center

questions.description: A candy whose name sounds like a kitchen accident, but it's made on purpose.
questions.question: This is leche quemada, a sweet made of cow's milk cooked with sugar. Its cousin, traditional cajeta from Celaya, is made with milk from which animal?
hints: Cajeta from Celaya, in Guanajuato, is famous all over Mexico
It's a small farm animal with a little beard
Its babies are called kids
questions.fun_fact: Cajeta gets its name from the little wooden boxes (cajitas) it used to be sold in.

media.credit: Cristina Zapata Pérez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cristina Zapata Pérez

questions.description: The flan's cousin who got all dressed up to go out.
questions.question: Which ingredient makes flan napolitano denser than classic flan?
hints: It's white and spreadable
It's made from milk and sold in the supermarket fridge
It comes in a little bar wrapped in silver foil
questions.fun_fact: Flan came to Mexico with the Spanish, and Mexicans made it their own with cajeta, cheese and even rompope.

media.credit: Cary Bass · CC BY-SA 2.5 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Cary Bass

questions.description: A stone that went to the trouble of painting itself on the inside.
questions.question: It's a stone with colored bands, it forms inside volcanic rock, and the finest marbles were once made from it. What stone is it?
hints: Its name comes from a river on the island of Sicily.
It forms layer by layer, like a stone onion.
In English, fine old-fashioned marbles were called “aggies” after it.
questions.fun_fact: Agate gets its bands because the mineral builds up layer by layer inside hollows in the rock.

media.credit: Photo by Tup Wanders · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Photo by Tup Wanders

questions.description: A Christmas party where even the front door gets its own lines.
questions.question: At the posadas, one group sings outside as pilgrims. Who do the people answering from inside the house play?
hints: They own the place where Joseph and Mary are looking for a bed.
At first they sing: “sigan adelante, yo no debo abrir” (“go on ahead, I must not open”).
In Spanish they're called “mesoneros,” from “mesón,” an old-time inn.
questions.fun_fact: At first the people inside reply “Aquí no es mesón, sigan adelante” (“This is no inn, go on ahead”), and only at the end, when they recognize Joseph and Mary, do they sing “Entren, santos peregrinos” (“Come in, holy pilgrims”).

media.credit: Nsaum75 at en.wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nsaum75 at en.wikipedia

questions.description: A date that isn't a holiday, but fires the starting gun for the season of ponche and piñatas.
questions.question: In Mexico, the posadas start on December 16 exactly. Why that day?
questions.answer: To have nine nights, like the months of pregnancy
wrong_answers: To have twelve nights, like the apostles
To have seven nights, like the days of Creation
To have forty nights, like Lent
hints: Each night, people go door to door singing to ask for shelter.
The posadas end right on Christmas Eve.
It's how long it takes for a baby to be born.
questions.fun_fact: The posadas come from the “misas de aguinaldo,” special Christmas masses the friars held in New Spain, as at the Acolman convent in the late 16th century.

media.credit: Donald Olszewski · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Donald Olszewski

questions.description: Outside, nothing but colored paper; inside, a secret almost nobody has seen.
questions.question: Traditionally, what was inside spiked piñatas like this one to hold the candy?
hints: Today almost all of them are made of cardboard and newspaper.
In the old days, they broke with a very loud sound.
It's a container also used in the kitchen for ponche or beans.
questions.fun_fact: According to tradition, the seven spikes of the piñata stand for the seven deadly sins, and breaking it means beating evil.

media.credit: jleonelss · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: jleonelss

questions.description: A miner with a stone slab on his back and more guts than a luchador at his first match.
questions.question: The Pípila Monument honors the miner who set fire to the door of the Alhóndiga de Granaditas. Whose army went in next?
hints: It was at the start of the War of Independence.
The Grito de Dolores had rung out that same month.
It was led by a priest.
questions.fun_fact: From the monument you can see all of Guanajuato, and you can ride a funicular up to it.

media.credit: August Dominus · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: August Dominus

questions.description: A name that sounds like a wild animal, but ends up in party clothes.
questions.question: On the coast of Oaxaca, some weavers use coyuchi in their huipiles. What is coyuchi?
hints: It comes from a plant, not from an animal or an insect.
Its color doesn't come from any dye.
It's a relative of the white fluff used to make manta cloth.
questions.fun_fact: Its name comes from Nahuatl and is linked to the coyote, because its color looks like the animal's fur.

media.credit: David.Clay.Photography · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: David.Clay.Photography

questions.description: Red, a little spicy, and more famous in Jalisco than many mariachi singers.
questions.question: Jalisco's sangrita is red and spicy, made with orange, chile, and pomegranate or tomato. What is it served for?
wrong_answers: To pour over tacos al pastor
hints: It's served in a small glass.
You sip it slowly, taking turns with another drink.
Its partner comes in a caballito.
questions.fun_fact: The original sangrita from Chapala had no tomato: its red color came from pomegranate and chile.

media.credit: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Francisco Javier Espinoza Pérez from Obregon, Mexico

questions.description: A soda that travels north and comes back a celebrity.
questions.question: In the United States, many people hunt for “Mexican Coke” in glass bottles because they say it tastes different. What is it sweetened with?
hints: It's a very old sweetener, much older than soda.
It comes from a tall plant grown in Veracruz.
It's the same sugar your grandma always used.
questions.fun_fact: In the United States, the regular version is sweetened with high-fructose corn syrup, which is why the Mexican one became famous.

media.credit: PattayaPatrol · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PattayaPatrol

questions.description: From general to supplier of inventions: the strangest career of the 19th century.
questions.question: Exiled in New York, Santa Anna gave Thomas Adams resin from a Mexican tree to make rubber. It didn't work. What did Adams invent with it?
hints: Adams turned his failed experiment into something cheap sold in every corner store.
The resin came from the chicozapote (sapodilla), a tree of the Maya forest.
In Mexico it's called chicle.
questions.fun_fact: Adams started selling his gum in the United States in the 1870s, and his last name became a famous brand.

media.credit: Adityamadhav83 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adityamadhav83

questions.description: Long before loudspeakers, the Mexica already had their own megaphone.
questions.question: In Aztec dance it is blown through the tip like a trumpet, and the Mexica played it to call people to ceremonies. What is this instrument made of?
hints: The Mexica had no cows or bulls.
It comes from an animal that lived in water.
It was brought from the coast, and it once had a resident who carried its house on its back.
questions.fun_fact: When the caracol (conch) is blown, players often greet the four directions: north, south, east and west.

media.credit: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Carlos Fonseca Mata

questions.description: Running shoes with zero cushioning and zero sports stores involved.
questions.question: Rarámuri runner Lorena Ramírez won ultramarathons in traditional huaraches. What are their soles made of?
hints: The Rarámuri make these huaraches themselves, from cheap materials they have at hand.
It is a recycled material that once had another use.
It comes from a car or a truck.
questions.fun_fact: In 2017, Lorena Ramírez won the Cerro Rojo ultramarathon, 50 km (31 miles) in Puebla, running in a skirt and huaraches.

media.credit: Robert FERREOL · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert FERREOL

questions.description: A necklace of natural swimming pools that a space rock left behind as a souvenir.
questions.question: In Yucatán, hundreds of cenotes form a huge ring that marks the edge of the buried Chicxulub crater. Roughly how wide is it?
hints: The asteroid that made it helped wipe out the dinosaurs.
The ring is too big to see from the ground.
Driving across it by road would take about two hours.
questions.fun_fact: The crater was found in the 1970s thanks to measurements taken while searching for oil; the ring of cenotes was linked to it later.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT

questions.description: A game so old the referee probably wore feathers.
questions.question: In the ball game the Mexica called tlachtli, the courts had stone rings like this one. What were they for?
questions.answer: To send the ball through them
wrong_answers: To tell the time by their shadow
hints: They were set high up on the walls of the court.
Players hit the rubber ball with their hips, not their hands.
Doing it was so hard that a player who managed it usually won the game on the spot.
questions.fun_fact: The ball was solid rubber and could weigh up to about 4 kg (9 lb), so players wore leather padding.

questions.question: The dancers in the Zócalo dance to a drum, with seed rattles on their ankles, and first they light copal. What is copal?

wrong_answers: A cacao seed roasted over a fire
A charcoal made from dried corncobs
A volcanic stone that glows when heated
hints: Peoples before the Spanish conquest already used it in their ceremonies.
It's also used on Day of the Dead altars.
It comes from a tree's bark, like a sap that hardens.
questions.fun_fact: The name copal comes from the Nahuatl word “copalli”, and the Aztecs were already burning it in their temples more than 500 years ago.

He's famous for the line “Respect for the rights of others is peace.”
questions.fun_fact: During the French intervention, Juárez carried the government across the country in a horse-drawn carriage, and today even a border city bears his name.

Frida Kahlo often wore this dress.
The women from there are called tehuanas.
questions.fun_fact: “La Llorona” has dozens of versions and every singer adds verses of their own; Chavela Vargas recorded one of the most famous.

questions.question: You're watching Disney and Pixar's “Coco”, and Miguel crosses a bridge of orange flowers. Which Mexican holiday is the movie set during?
hints: For this holiday, people set up altars with family photos.
People eat a special bread and little sugar skulls.
It is celebrated on November 1 and 2.
questions.fun_fact: “Coco” won two Oscars in 2018: Best Animated Feature and Best Original Song for “Remember Me”.

media.author: Dave Fey from St. Louis, USA

questions.description: A language that lives so high up it can almost chat with the clouds.
questions.question: It’s spoken in the Sierra Norte of Oaxaca, its speakers call themselves “ayuuk,” and their sacred mountain is Zempoaltépetl. Which language is it?
hints: It is not the most widely spoken Indigenous language in Oaxaca.
Its towns, like Tlahuitoltepec, are famous for their brass bands.
Its name looks like that of another Oaxacan language, but it’s shorter.
questions.fun_fact: “Ayuuk” is often translated as “the language of the mountain” or “the flowery word.”

media.author: Prsjl

questions.description: A year so strange that even Mexican soccer changed its own rules.
questions.question: In 2020, during the pandemic, Liga MX created the Liga de Expansión. What did it suspend in exchange?
hints: The decision made the weakest teams happy.
The move was meant to ease the clubs' money troubles during the crisis.
The last-place team no longer dropped down a division.
questions.fun_fact: Before the pause, relegation was decided by the “tabla de cocientes”, which averaged a team's points over its last few seasons.

media.author: Own work

questions.description: The woman from Sonora who got all of Mexico up off the couch.
questions.question: Complete it: Usain Bolt is to the 100 meters as Ana Gabriela Guevara is to…
hints: She was born in Sonora and also played basketball when she was young.
It's a longer distance than Bolt's, but still a sprint.
Guevara became world champion in this event in Paris in 2003.
questions.fun_fact: Ana Gabriela Guevara, from Nogales, Sonora, won Olympic silver at Athens 2004.

questions.description: Architecture so modern for its time that more than one neighbor in San Ángel thought it was a factory.
questions.question: Two studio houses, one blue and one red and white, joined by a rooftop bridge, designed by Juan O'Gorman in San Ángel. What museum are they today?
questions.answer: Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo Studio House
hints: They were built in 1931–1932, when “functionalist” houses were brand new.
A very famous painter couple lived there, each in their own house.
He painted in the big house; she painted in the blue one.
questions.fun_fact: The fence around the houses is made of organ pipe cactus, a very Mexican living wall.

media.author: José Luiz

questions.description: Four worlds came before this one, and none of them came with an extended warranty.
questions.question: According to the Mexica, the first sun was called Nahui Océlotl. Fill in what its name means: “Four ___”.
hints: Each sun was named after a date in the calendar: a number and a sign.
Tezcatlipoca ruled that first world, and giants lived in it.
At the end of that age, the giants were eaten by the same animal that gives the sun its name.
questions.fun_fact: On the Sun Stone, the four earlier suns appear around the central face, each in its own box.

media.author: El Comandante

questions.description: A piece of wood that is the most important guest at a Veracruz party.
questions.question: At a son jarocho fandango, what is the wooden tarima for?
questions.answer: To stomp on so it sounds like a drum
wrong_answers: For the musicians to sit on while playing
To hold the town's food offerings
For the verse singers to read their coplas
hints: At a fandango, the dance is also part of the music.
The hollow wood booms with every hit.
Dancers mark the rhythm on top of it with their heels.
questions.fun_fact: At many fandangos the tarima counts as one more instrument, and the dancers “play” it with their feet.

media.credit: Koffermejia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Koffermejia

questions.description: A band with a name straight out of the zoo and a fandango soul.
questions.question: Complete the name of the band founded by Gilberto Gutiérrez that has revived jarocho fandangos since 1977: Mono…
hints: It was a key band of the jarana movement in Veracruz.
Its founder was born in southern Veracruz.
It's the color of traditional jarocho clothing.
questions.fun_fact: Mono Blanco helped bring son jarocho back to community fandangos, not just concert stages.

media.credit: Koffermejia · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Koffermejia

questions.description: For people who want to be at every party at the same time.
questions.question: Which Spanish saying warns that if you take on too many things at once, you won't do any of them well?
questions.answer: El que mucho abarca poco aprieta
wrong_answers: No por mucho madrugar amanece más temprano
Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente
El que con lobos anda a aullar se enseña
hints: It isn't about schedules or bad company.
It compares someone trying to carry too many things with someone who can no longer hold them tight.
Its first verb means to wrap your arms around something: “abar…”.
questions.fun_fact: “Abarcar” comes from Latin, and its root has to do with arms: to “abarcar” is to wrap your arms around something.

questions.description: A state so tiny you can cover it on the map with a coin.
questions.question: Look at the map: the highlighted state is the smallest in Mexico. Which one is it?
hints: It is in the center of the country, very close to the capital.
It borders Puebla, which almost surrounds it.
Its capital has the same name as the state.
questions.fun_fact: Online, there is a famous joke that “Tlaxcala doesn't exist,” even though it is one of the states with the most history in the country.

questions.description: A hundred episodes of tears, secrets and slaps… all just to get to this.
questions.question: In a classic telenovela, the truth comes out and the villain gets what she deserves. What scene usually closes the last episode?
hints: It's a party with lots of guests.
There's almost always a cake with several tiers.
The heroine walks to the altar dressed in white.
questions.fun_fact: Some telenovelas have filmed alternate endings so that nobody could leak how the story ends.

questions.description: Faces that dance once a year and spend the rest of the time resting on the wall.
questions.question: Many dance masks from Guerrero are made by hand and painted in bright colors. What are they usually made of?
hints: Each craftsman gives it his own style, and no two masks ever come out the same.
The mask is light and gets several coats of paint and varnish.
It comes from a tree trunk.
questions.fun_fact: Many dance masks are handed down from parents to children and danced in for decades.

questions.description: A little square of cloth that's for flirting on the dance floor and for something far less elegant at home.
questions.question: Look at the photo: many Mexican dancers wave this while they dance. What is it used for at home?
hints: You can keep it in your pocket.
You use it when you have a cold.
You hold it up to your face when you sneeze.
questions.fun_fact: In many Mexican sones, dancers wave a handkerchief to flirt with their partner.

questions.description: There was a time when understanding things cost exactly twenty centavos.
questions.question: When you finally understand something, you say «¡ya me cayó el veinte!». That veinte was a 20-centavo coin. What did it drop into?
hints: It was a machine you found out on the street.
Sometimes the coin got stuck, and you had to wait for it to drop.
Before cell phones, people lined up on the corner to use it.
questions.fun_fact: Sometimes the coin was slow to drop, so you had to wait or give the machine a little tap, which is why people say the veinte “took a while to drop.”

hints: It is a city in northern Mexico.
It is an industrial city surrounded by mountains.
Its nickname is “la Sultana del Norte.”

questions.question: When did work begin on Mérida's Paseo de Montejo, the avenue inspired by the Champs-Élysées in Paris?

Porfirio Díaz was in power, and he loved all things French.
The mansions were paid for with henequen money, before 1900.
questions.fun_fact: The Paseo de Montejo was first laid out in 1888, when henequen made Yucatán one of the richest places in Mexico.

hints: Think about which days telenovelas air on regular broadcast TV.
On weekends, the TV schedule changes.
You have to wait for the new week to start.
questions.fun_fact: Many writers save the biggest cliffhanger for Friday, so you won't switch channels on Monday.

questions.description: The Mexican science of deciding who gets the front seat of the car.
questions.question: It's shouted before a coin toss to decide who goes first, and each word is one side of the coin. What do people say in Mexico?
hints: Other countries say it differently.
One side of the coin has the national coat of arms.
One of the words is a bird that's on the flag.
questions.fun_fact: The “sol” part comes from old coins that showed a cap with rays, like a sun.

The show started in 2002.
It's a singing reality show from Televisa's big rival.
questions.fun_fact: “La Academia”, which started in 2002, launched singers such as Yuridia.

hints: Paz was about 35 years old.
A year later, “The Labyrinth of Solitude” came out.
It was just before the middle of the 20th century.

He almost always appeared with a ball at his feet.

It is the country's capital.

questions.question: Between 1917 and 1922, a Mexican anthropologist uncovered this temple in Teotihuacan's Ciudadela and studied the whole valley in depth. Who was he?
hints: He was a student of Franz Boas at Columbia University.
He's called the father of Mexican anthropology; he also studied Mexican migration to the United States.
In 1914 he found the first remains of the Templo Mayor, decades before its big excavation.
questions.fun_fact: His work “The Population of the Valley of Teotihuacan” (1922) was groundbreaking because it studied the ruins, the history and the lives of the people living there all together.

questions.description: A language that came down from the clouds and settled in the Isthmus for good.
questions.question: You're at the market in Juchitán and hear people speaking Zapotec. How many people in Mexico speak a Zapotec language?
hints: It's one of the most widely spoken Indigenous languages in Mexico.
It's far more than the people of one town, but fewer than all of Oaxaca.
The number is close to half a million.
questions.fun_fact: The Isthmus Zapotecs call themselves binnizá, which translates as “people of the clouds.”

questions.description: A city so hot that even the baseballs break a sweat.
questions.question: Its baseball team has won the most Mexican Pacific League titles, it's a state capital, and summers top 45 °C (113 °F). Which city is it?
hints: It's in the northwest of the country, near the desert.
It's the capital of Sonora.
Its team is named after people who grow or sell oranges.
questions.fun_fact: The Naranjeros have also won the Caribbean Series, for example in 2014.

questions.description: A place that has a life-size twin in the big city.

hints: I am a Maya city.

My name means “painted walls” in Maya.
questions.fun_fact: Rina Lazo also painted “Venerable abuelo maíz” (Venerable Grandfather Corn), the mural in the Maya Hall of the National Museum of Anthropology.

questions.description: Three plants that share a home and actually get along.
questions.question: Corn, beans and squash are planted together: the beans climb the corn stalks and the squash covers the ground. What is this field called?
hints: It's a way of farming that comes from Mesoamerica.
Its name comes from Nahuatl.
It's the word farmers use for their cornfield.
questions.fun_fact: Corn, beans and squash grown together are also known as “the three sisters.”

They came a few years after the War of Independence ended.
It was in the 1820s.
questions.fun_fact: Decades later, the Cornish mining community also brought soccer to Pachuca, which is why it's called the “cradle of Mexican soccer.”

questions.question: It has corn, carrots, zucchini and a good marrow bone, and it's called caldo de res. Which animal does carne de res come from?
hints: It's a big farm animal.
It eats grass all day in the fields.
It also gives us milk.
questions.fun_fact: Marrow is the soft part inside the bone, and lots of people fight over it in the soup.

hints: They dance with little hops to the beat of a brass band.
They wear masks with beards that point upward and huge hats.
They are the symbol of the carnival in Tepoztlán, Yautepec and Tlayacapan.
questions.fun_fact: Legend says the chinelos began as Indigenous people's way of mocking the bearded Spaniards who wouldn't let them celebrate carnival.

An allegory is a way of showing something through figures and symbols.
Each float tells something: a story, a character or the carnival's theme.
questions.fun_fact: The Veracruz Carnival boasts of being “the happiest in the world” and lasts several days, with parades along the malecón (seafront).

Its name comes from Nahuatl and has to do with deer.
questions.fun_fact: In Mazatlán, total darkness lasted about 4 minutes and 20 seconds.

They were made of something that comes from trees.

In their country, the Republicans were fighting Franco's side.

The Chivas play there.

Its home city has a very famous soccer team that plays in white.
It was born in Madrid.

My name is the Spanish word for a baseball bat.

questions.description: A money plan for the whole year that you won't find in any economics book.

Your socks go there too.

You count it in pesos.

A prayer said nine days in a row

It hits whoever ate too much or ate something heavy.

My name includes a European country.

It's long and pink.

It's celebrated every September 16.

My name has only four letters, and I'm a boy, not a girl.
My name rhymes with “photo”.

Here come the runny nose and the sneezing.
It's that illness with chills, a cough and a stuffy nose.

Purple for love and brown for money

Its name comes from Greek, and it's also used for monuments in Egypt and Greece.

It's more than 100 meters long, but less than 200.

They are the same people who built Chichén Itzá.
