media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: The very first Google Maps, with little footprints instead of arrows.
questions.question: This Mexica codex tells the journey from Aztlán, with footprints marking the way. What is it called?
hints: It is a long strip of amate bark paper that folds like an accordion.
It carries the surname of an 18th-century Italian collector.
It is also known as the Tira de la Peregrinación (Strip of the Pilgrimage).
questions.fun_fact: The Codex Boturini is more than 5 m (16 ft) long and is kept at the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City.

media.credit: Unknown (codex) - El Comandante (photographer) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Unknown (codex) - El Comandante (photographer)

questions.description: Some people show up early to the party, and some show up before the invitations go out.
questions.question: In Cuchillo Parado, Chihuahua, Toribio Ortega took up arms before the date Madero had set. On what day?
hints: Madero had called for the uprising to begin one November day at six in the evening.
Ortega jumped the gun by less than a week.
It was six days before Revolution Day.
questions.fun_fact: Because of that early uprising, Cuchillo Parado calls itself “the cradle of the Revolution.”

media.credit: William L. Farr · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: William L. Farr

questions.description: A saying that crosses the finish line without breaking a sweat.
questions.question: Like the tortoise in the fable, this saying favors going slow and steady over rushing ahead. Which saying is it?
questions.answer: Más vale paso que dure y no trote que canse
wrong_answers: Camarón que se duerme se lo lleva la corriente
Al que madruga, Dios lo ayuda
A caballo regalado no se le mira el colmillo
hints: It fits long tasks, like studying for a test or going on a long hike.
It warns you not to use up all your energy at the start.
It names two of a horse's gaits: a slow one and a faster one.
questions.fun_fact: Horses have several gaits, or ways of moving: the walk, the trot and the gallop are the best known.

media.credit: Ide8sion · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ide8sion

questions.description: A short nickname for people who never stop bragging about their hometown.
questions.question: In Mexico, who gets called “regio”?
hints: It comes from a longer word for the people of a city.
It's a northern city, famous for carne asada and its mountains.
Its symbol is the Cerro de la Silla.
questions.fun_fact: “Regio” comes from “regiomontano”, which sounds like Latin for “king's mountain”, just like Monterrey.

media.credit: Juan Emilio Prades Bel · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Juan Emilio Prades Bel

questions.description: When the notebook gets too small, history class goes up on the wall.
questions.question: After the Revolution, José Vasconcelos had Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros paint history on the walls of public buildings. Mainly for whom?
hints: The murals were painted in schools, markets and palaces, where anyone could see them.
In those years, most Mexicans had never gone to school.
You can understand a mural just by looking at it, without any words.
questions.fun_fact: Diego Rivera's mural on the staircase of the Palacio Nacional has hundreds of figures and took him several years to finish.

media.credit: Drkgk · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Drkgk

questions.description: When there's no hospital nearby, someone has to invent one out of bandages and courage.
questions.question: Leonor Villegas de Magnón founded it in Laredo in 1913, and its nurses cared for wounded soldiers on Carranza's side. What was it called?
hints: Its name sounds like a much more famous international organization.
It cared for Constitutionalist soldiers on the border.
Its color is the same as the flag you wave to ask for peace.
questions.fun_fact: Leonor Villegas de Magnón wrote a memoir, “The Rebel,” which came out decades after her death.

media.credit: Billy Hathorn at en.wikipedia · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Billy Hathorn at en.wikipedia

questions.description: A trip back in time to a theater where the show ran for weeks and the script was a whole country.
questions.question: You're in a theater in Querétaro, listening to deputy Francisco J. Múgica argue for secular education for everyone. What years are these?
hints: A Constitutional Congress met in that theater.
Venustiano Carranza was the leader of the country.
The Constitution written there is still in force in Mexico.
questions.fun_fact: Years later, Múgica helped Lázaro Cárdenas write the speech announcing the oil expropriation.

media.credit: Own work · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Own work

questions.description: A movie so expensive it nearly bankrupted the people who made it.
questions.question: Who directed “¡Vámonos con Pancho Villa!” (Let's Go with Pancho Villa!), a classic of 1930s Mexican cinema?
hints: The same director made “El compadre Mendoza.”
He also directed “Allá en el Rancho Grande,” which paved the way for the comedia ranchera.
His surname is the Spanish word for the fountains in a town square.
questions.fun_fact: The film cost so much that it nearly ruined the studio, and for years it was seen as a box-office flop.

media.credit: D.W. Hoffman, an El Paso photographer · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: D.W. Hoffman, an El Paso photographer

questions.description: A saying with more style than a fashion show in the middle of the jungle.
questions.question: Someone shows up super dressed up, and people tell them: «Aunque la mona se vista de seda…». How does it end?
hints: The saying means clothes don't change who you are.
People say it when someone tries to look like something they're not.
It ends by saying the monkey doesn't change: she stays just as she is.
questions.fun_fact: Silk is made by silkworms, which spin their cocoons from a single thread that can be hundreds of meters long.

media.credit: Daniel Aufgang · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniel Aufgang

questions.description: You survived secundaria and the entrance exam; now it's time for a brand-new uniform.
questions.question: In Mexico, if you go to a CBTIS after secundaria, what kind of school are you in?
hints: It belongs to the SEP, and there are hundreds across the country.
The students there are about 15 to 18 years old.
The T in its initials stands for “Tecnológico”.
questions.fun_fact: CBTIS stands for Centro de Bachillerato Tecnológico Industrial y de Servicios, and many of its students also graduate as technicians.

media.credit: Nikolina Šepić · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nikolina Šepić

questions.description: This phrase shoots out every time someone shares the gossip of the year.
questions.question: You shout me when someone tells you something unbelievable. I sound like I'm calling them a liar, but I only show surprise. What expression am I?
hints: You hear it all the time among Mexican teens.
It's a close cousin of “¡No manches!”.
Its verb is the thing Thomas Edison was famous for doing.
questions.fun_fact: “¡No inventes!” works for good and bad surprises alike: winning a prize or a pop quiz.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: A nickname that saves a lot of money on shampoo.
questions.question: In Mexico, what fond nickname do people give someone with no hair at all?
hints: The nickname describes the head.
Newborn babies sometimes get called this too.
It sounds like the word “pelo” (hair) with a bigger ending.
questions.fun_fact: In Mexican nicknames, “chino” has nothing to do with China: it's what you call someone with curly hair.

media.credit: Wilfredor · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wilfredor

questions.description: A chilango phrase that sounds like someone just greeted their aunt in the middle of the street.
questions.question: It's said when you're fed up, it's classic Mexico City slang, and it ends with the nickname for women named Soledad. What expression is it?
hints: You use it to ask someone to stop doing something.
It's said in a tired voice, stretching out the last word.
It starts with “ya” and ends with a name.
questions.fun_fact: “Chole” is the traditional nickname for Soledad, just as “Lupe” is for Guadalupe and “Chucho” for Jesús.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: A song so good that a whole telenovela took its name.
questions.question: Which Mexican singer-songwriter wrote “Te sigo amando,” the theme song of the telenovela with the same name?
hints: He's one of the most famous songwriters in Mexican music.
He wrote “Amor eterno” and “Querida.”
He was nicknamed “El Divo de Juárez.”
questions.fun_fact: Juan Gabriel wrote more than 1,500 songs, and many of them were recorded by other artists.

media.credit: A S M Jobaer · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: A S M Jobaer

questions.description: Feathers that have never seen a bird fly up close.
questions.question: Look at the photo: which dancers wear this on their heads?
hints: They dance to the beat of a big drum.
You often see them in the Zócalo in Mexico City.
They're also called “Aztec dancers.”
questions.fun_fact: Conchero headdresses often have pheasant or ostrich feathers, which can sway a lot during the dance.

media.credit: Jonata Oregón · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jonata Oregón

questions.description: If you're house hunting, don't move onto this lady's street.
questions.question: In Francisco Hinojosa's book, the worst lady in the world is so mean that everyone flees the town. What is the town called?
hints: The book begins by saying she lived in the north of this town.
It isn't a real town: the author made it up.
Its name starts with T and has three syllables.
questions.fun_fact: “La peor señora del mundo” (The Worst Lady in the World) came out in 1992 and is one of the Mexican children's books most read in schools.

media.credit: Internet Archive Book Images · No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Internet Archive Book Images

questions.description: A dog so bald it never has to go to the groomer.
questions.question: Dante, the dog in “Coco”, is a hairless Mexican breed and one of the oldest in the Americas, over 3,000 years old. Which breed is it?
hints: Its name comes from Nahuatl.
The Mexica believed it guided souls to Mictlán.
Lots of people lovingly call it “xolo”.
questions.fun_fact: Because it has almost no hair, a xolo's skin feels warm, and people once used it to warm up the sick.

media.credit: Yavidaxiu · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yavidaxiu

questions.description: A case of mistaken identity worthy of a telenovela.
questions.question: The American badger lives in northern Mexico and belongs to the weasel family. Which of these animals is NOT in that family?
hints: The answer has a ringed tail.
It's a close relative of the raccoon.
In many parts of Mexico this animal is also called “tejón”.
questions.fun_fact: The American badger sometimes hunts as a team with the coyote: one digs into the burrows and the other catches the prey that runs out.

media.credit: Yathin S Krishnappa · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Yathin S Krishnappa

questions.description: A bird that never makes it onto the postcards, but works harder than anyone.
questions.question: This black bird has a bald head, circles in the sky looking for dead animals, and its Mexican name comes from Nahuatl. What is it?
hints: It has no feathers on its head so it stays clean while eating.
You see groups of them over garbage dumps and highways.
In English it's called the black vulture.
questions.fun_fact: Its stomach juices are so acidic that they kill germs that would make almost any other animal sick.

media.credit: ゴスロリ · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ゴスロリ

questions.description: In cartoons it only says “beep beep,” but in real life it's very hungry.
questions.question: In northern Mexico the roadrunner is also called “paisano.” It runs at about 30 km/h (20 mph) across the desert. What does it catch with that speed?
hints: It eats meat.
Its food has scales.
It even takes on rattlesnakes.
questions.fun_fact: Even though it prefers running, the roadrunner can fly, just not very far.

media.credit: BLMArizona · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: BLMArizona

questions.description: The only time a boxer is more scared of a scale than of the other guy.
questions.question: The day before a fight, boxers step on a scale in front of the press and fans. What is this weigh-in for?
questions.answer: To check they make their division’s weight
wrong_answers: To decide who walks out to the ring first
To work out how much money each one earns
To choose the color of their gloves
hints: Boxing has strawweight, lightweight, middleweight, heavyweight...
If a boxer comes in too heavy, he can lose the title or pay a fine.
It’s about how many kilos are allowed.
questions.fun_fact: After the weigh-in, many boxers put several kilos back on before stepping into the ring the next day.

media.credit: Nikodem Nijaki · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Nikodem Nijaki

questions.description: His nickname tells you which hand he hits with, but not where he comes from.
questions.question: Gilberto “Zurdo” Ramírez is from Sinaloa, and in 2016 he became the first Mexican super middleweight world champion. Which city is he from?
hints: It's a city by the sea.
It's famous for its malecón (seaside boardwalk) and its carnival.
It's called “the Pearl of the Pacific.”
questions.fun_fact: Years later, “Zurdo” moved up in weight and also became a cruiserweight world champion.

media.credit: Compitaa6803 · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Compitaa6803

questions.description: A few tacos too many and suddenly you’re in a different classroom.
questions.question: A lightweight boxer puts on a few kilos and moves up to the next division. Which one is it?
hints: Above lightweight, the divisions go up just a few kilos at a time.
The limit for this division is about 63.5 kg (140 lb).
Put a superhero’s prefix in front of the old division’s name.
questions.fun_fact: Julio César Chávez was a world champion at super featherweight, lightweight and super lightweight.

media.credit: Ethan Long · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ethan Long

questions.description: A bedtime bribe so the baby finally closes those little eyes.
questions.question: It's sung softly, asks the baby to fall asleep and promises something for when they wake up. In “Duérmete mi niño,” what will the baby get?
hints: It's something to drink.
It's served nice and warm in a clay mug (jarro).
It's made with corn dough and is sometimes flavored like champurrado.
questions.fun_fact: People in Mexico have been drinking atole since before the Spanish arrived.

media.credit: Hu Nhu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hu Nhu

questions.description: A newborn baby who already wants a driver.
questions.question: In the lullaby “Este niño lindo”, the baby wants to be taken for a ride in a car. When was he born?
hints: It’s a lullaby to put the baby to sleep.
In Spanish, the answer rhymes with “coche” (car).
It’s when the moon and stars come out.
questions.fun_fact: In another verse, the baby who was “born in the daytime” wants to be taken to the candy shop.

media.credit: Paul Goyette from Chicago, USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Paul Goyette from Chicago, USA

questions.description: A retreat that ended with a gold medal.
questions.question: You're in Otumba, where Cortés and his men, fleeing after the Noche Triste, defeated a huge Mexica army. In what year was it?
hints: It was in the 16th century.
Cortés had arrived in Mexico the year before.
Tenochtitlan fell the following year.
questions.fun_fact: According to the chronicles, the battle was decided when Cortés brought down the Mexica captain carrying the battle standard.

media.credit: Thelmadatter · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thelmadatter

questions.description: A patio where the mules worked harder than kids do at recess.
questions.question: In the patio process, invented in Pachuca around 1555, what was ground ore mixed with to separate out the silver?
hints: Mules and horses trampled the mixture for weeks.
It was scarce and expensive, the Spanish Crown controlled its trade, and much of it came by ship from Spain.
In colonial times it was called “azogue”.
questions.fun_fact: The method was invented by Bartolomé de Medina from Seville, and it helped silver from New Spain travel across half the world.

media.credit: José Luiz · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: José Luiz

questions.description: He painted so well that even the saints sat perfectly still for him.
questions.question: I was born in Oaxaca, led one of the first painting academies in New Spain and painted series of casta paintings. My portrait of Sor Juana is the most famous one. Who am I?
hints: I lived in the 18th century.
I wrote “Maravilla americana”, a book about the image of the Virgin of Guadalupe.
I share my first name with the boy from “Coco”.
questions.fun_fact: In 1751, Cabrera was one of the painters who examined the tilma of the Virgin of Guadalupe up close.

media.credit: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada

questions.description: A name you see in every corner tiendita, even if you've never stopped to read it.
questions.question: In Mexico, Bonafont is a well-known brand of…
hints: You drink it, you don't eat it.
It's sold in small bottles and also in big garrafones.
It's what you crave most after running in the sun.
questions.fun_fact: Bonafont belongs to Danone, the same French company that makes many of the yogurts at the supermarket.

media.credit: Wolfgang Sauber · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Wolfgang Sauber

questions.description: A question that tastes like the garden and an answer that tastes like an ice-cold pitcher.
questions.question: If someone asks you “¿Qué te pasa, calabaza?”, how does the answer “Nada, nada…” end?
hints: It has to rhyme with “nada”.
It's a cool drink for hot days.
It's made with water, sugar and a sour green fruit.
questions.fun_fact: Squash is native to Mesoamerica and has been grown in Mexico for about 10,000 years.

media.credit: Richard Humphrey · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Richard Humphrey

questions.description: A Cuban star who crossed the Gulf of Mexico to shine in Mexican cinema.
questions.question: I was born in Guanabacoa, Cuba, and was nicknamed “La Única”. In Mexico I played Mercé, the nanny in “Angelitos negros”, with Pedro Infante. Who am I?
hints: I was a singer, pianist and actress.
I was one of the first to record “El manisero” (“The Peanut Vendor”).
My last name sounds a bit like “mountaineer”.
questions.fun_fact: The great Bola de Nieve started his career as her accompanying pianist.

media.credit: Libby norman · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Libby norman

questions.description: The room with the best view in the house, though nobody brags about it.
questions.question: Many old buildings in Mexico City have small rooms on the rooftop, each with its own bathroom. Who were they built for?
hints: Someone who worked in the building lived there.
That person helped the family with cleaning and cooking.
On the building plans they were called “cuartos de servicio.”
questions.fun_fact: Today many of these rooftop rooms are rented to students or have become small artists' studios.

media.credit: Daniel Case · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Daniel Case

questions.description: Where every house is a twin and the guard knows your license plate by heart.
questions.question: Rows of identical houses, a guard booth at the gate and sometimes a shared pool. What is this kind of neighborhood called in Mexico?
hints: It's very common on the edges of cities.
A builder splits a big piece of land into many lots.
Its name comes from dividing something into fractions.
questions.fun_fact: In northern Mexico, many fraccionamientos have English names or names of faraway places, like “Villas de Toscana”.

media.credit: Andre Carrotflower · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Andre Carrotflower

questions.description: The family of sauce-covered tortillas has lots of cousins, and all their last names start with “en-.”
questions.question: They're folded tortillas with queso fresco and cream, covered in tomato sauce instead of chile sauce. What is this dish called?
hints: Look closely at what the sauce is made of.
Its name comes from the sauce's main ingredient, not from chile.
Its name hides the Spanish word for tomato.
questions.fun_fact: Mexico has a whole family of dishes named this way: enchiladas, enfrijoladas, enmoladas and entomatadas.

media.credit: Armando Gómez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Armando Gómez

questions.description: A Latin last name shared by one very spicy family.
questions.question: I'm a Latin name: I group the jalapeño, the habanero and the bell pepper, and Mexico has grown me for thousands of years. Which plant genus am I?
hints: Botanists put all chiles under my name.
I'm not the one for black pepper or the one for onions.
The substance that makes chiles hot is named after me.
questions.fun_fact: Capsaicin, the stuff that makes chiles hot, takes its name from the genus Capsicum.

media.credit: Bhaskaranaidu · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bhaskaranaidu

questions.description: What's left of the elote when there's no elote left.
questions.question: You finish your elote and you're left with the olote, the hard core with no kernels. In the countryside, what has it traditionally been used for?
hints: It has no kernels left, so it's no good for making masa.
Once dry, it becomes light and hard.
It burns well along with firewood.
questions.fun_fact: The word «olote» comes from Nahuatl, just like «elote».

media.credit: Tomascastelazo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Tomascastelazo

questions.description: A flower that guards the door better than a watchdog.
questions.question: Take a close look: this plant tastes like anise, and in Morelos people make crosses from its flowers on September 28. What is it called?
hints: Its flowers are small and yellow.
It's a cousin of cempasúchil, but it isn't the Day of the Dead flower.
The crosses go up on the eve of Saint Michael's Day to protect homes and milpas.
questions.fun_fact: Pericón is also called “Mexican tarragon” because it tastes a lot like tarragon.

media.credit: Traper Bemowski · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Traper Bemowski

questions.description: An actor who worked nights and slept all day, strictly because the role demanded it.
questions.question: Which Spanish-born actor played Count Lavud in the Mexican horror film “El vampiro” (The Vampire, 1957)?
hints: He was almost unknown when he took the role.
He was born in Gijón and moved to Mexico as a young man.
His last name is the Spanish word for oak trees.
questions.fun_fact: Germán Robles was one of the first movie vampires to show fangs, a year before Christopher Lee's British Dracula.

media.credit: Jorge Royan · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jorge Royan

questions.description: A man who gave bolero its squeakiest little voice… on guitar.
questions.question: In 1944 in New York, I formed one of the most famous bolero trios in the world and gave bolero its small, high-pitched guitar, the requinto. Who am I?
hints: People called me “el Güero.”
My trio was called Los Panchos.
My last name has three letters.
questions.fun_fact: The requinto is smaller than a regular guitar and sounds higher, which makes it perfect for the fancy runs in a bolero.

media.credit: Jo Dusepo · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Jo Dusepo

questions.description: A horoscope so serious they painted it by hand, with priests as witnesses.
questions.question: The tonalámatl, the Mexica “book of fates,” recorded a ritual calendar. How many days did that calendar have?
hints: It’s shorter than a solar year.
The Maya had a calendar with the same number of days: the tzolkin.
It combines 20 day signs with the numbers 1 to 13.
questions.fun_fact: The 260-day calendar was called the tonalpohualli, and it was used to choose babies’ names.

media.credit: Rosemania · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Rosemania

questions.description: Before becoming king, every tlatoani was just the kid getting scolded at home.
questions.question: Huitzilíhuitl, the second tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, was the son of the first. What was his father's name?
hints: He ruled from the late 14th century.
His name means “handful of reeds.”
His name starts with “A” and ends in “-tli.”
questions.fun_fact: The name Huitzilíhuitl means “hummingbird feather.”

media.credit: Patolocosi · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Patolocosi

questions.description: The ancient figures that always look good in photos.
questions.question: The clay “caritas sonrientes” (smiling faces) from central Veracruz, in the El Tajín region: from which era are they?
hints: They are from the same time as El Tajín at its peak.
They were made several centuries before the Spanish arrived, but long after the Olmecs.
They are between 1,100 and 1,400 years old.
questions.fun_fact: Many have open mouths and raised arms, as if singing or dancing, and nobody knows for sure why they smile.

media.credit: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Arian Zwegers from Brussels, Belgium

questions.description: A song for slow dancing up close, even in the middle of a rock concert.
questions.question: It's by Maldita Vecindad, it came out on the 1991 album “El Circo,” and it's slow and tropical, with a saxophone. What's it called?
hints: It's one of the best-loved songs of 1990s Mexican rock.
Its title is repeated over and over in the chorus.
Its name sounds like “cumbia,” but it starts with a K.
questions.fun_fact: “El Circo” is considered one of the most important albums in Spanish-language rock.

media.credit: PattayaPatrol · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PattayaPatrol

questions.description: Long before memes, neighborhood rockers were already inventing their own language.
questions.question: You're at the Tianguis del Chopo among leather jackets and El Tri records. What were the young neighborhood rockers of the 1980s called?
hints: The name comes from what they called each other: their crew of buddies.
Their music was the rock urbano heard in the working-class neighborhoods of Mexico City.
The word for “gang of friends” comes right after “chavo”.
questions.fun_fact: The Tianguis Cultural del Chopo has been held every Saturday since the 1980s and is a meeting point for rockers.

media.credit: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ProtoplasmaKid

questions.description: Three voices opened a box… and out came ballads.
questions.question: In which decade did Pandora, the trio behind “¿Cómo te va mi amor?”, release their first album?
hints: It's a trio made up only of women.
People were still listening to music on cassettes and vinyl records.
They started around the same years as Timbiriche and Flans.
questions.fun_fact: Pandora was formed by Isabel Lascurain and the sisters Mayte and Fernanda Meade.

media.credit: fancycrave1 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: fancycrave1

questions.description: A telenovela in a red tie that came from very far away.
questions.question: The telenovela “Rebelde,” which gave us RBD, is the Mexican version of another teen series. Which country is the original from?
hints: The original premiered in 2002.
It's a South American country.
Its capital is Buenos Aires.
questions.fun_fact: The original series was called “Rebelde Way” and was created by Cris Morena.

media.credit: PattayaPatrol · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PattayaPatrol

questions.description: Grandma's medicine: it doesn't come from the drugstore, it comes in a deep bowl.
questions.question: This warm soup is the home remedy when you catch a cold. Which bird's meat goes in it?
hints: It's a farm bird.
It lays eggs almost every day.
It's the mother of the little chicks.
questions.fun_fact: Caldo de gallina is often tastier than chicken soup because a hen is an older bird, and its meat cooks slowly.

media.credit: Gonza Rizzo · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gonza Rizzo

questions.description: A son so elegant that even the embroidered skirts get nervous when it starts.
questions.question: La Sandunga, danced in the traje de tehuana on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, is sung in Spanish and in…

hints: It was already the 21st century.
It came out the same year as “La leyenda de la Llorona”.
It was early in the 2010s.

questions.description: You can't go to the movies in pajamas, but here it almost feels like your own living room.

questions.answer: Seats that move and splash you with water
wrong_answers: A waiter who brings you your food
A menu of dishes and drinks
hints: The VIP theater is about being comfortable and relaxed.
There they spoil you with food, not with scares.
Moving and getting wet belongs to another kind of theater, more adventure than rest.

questions.description: Grandma's favorite drink, served in her favorite cup.
questions.question: Café de olla is made with cinnamon and piloncillo and served in a traditional jarrito (small mug). What is the jarrito made of?
hints: It's a material that comes from the ground.
It's shaped while wet and then fired in a kiln.
Traditional pots and water jugs are made of the same thing.
questions.fun_fact: Many people say the clay gives café de olla an earthy taste it doesn't have in any other cup.

To put them on the dogs

They're a gift for someone who is no longer here.
They go on the headstone or right next to it.

San Andrés Huayápam holds a fair in my honor.
My name starts with the same two letters as “tequila”.
questions.fun_fact: Tejate is beaten by hand, and the foam from the cacao flower rises to the top on its own.

hints: It's in Oaxaca, near the Pacific coast.
It's famous for its velas (big all-night fiestas) and its muxes.
Its official name ends in “de Zaragoza”.
questions.fun_fact: Natalia Toledo won the Nezahualcóyotl Prize for Literature in Mexican Languages in 2004 with her poetry book “Olivo negro” (Black Olive).

questions.description: So pretty you'd feel bad stepping on them with muddy shoes.

hints: It comes from an animal.
It's the same fiber used in many sarapes.
It's sheared once a year.

In this match, each one bets their mask against the other's.
The winner leaves the ring just the way they came in.
questions.fun_fact: Whoever loses a mask-against-mask match has to say their real name in front of the crowd.

The “molli” part is also in the name of a very Mexican party dish.

questions.fun_fact: The name of mole comes from that same Nahuatl word, “molli.”

On top of that temple stand huge statues called atlantes.

Our city was very powerful between the years 900 and 1150.
Our capital was called Tollan.

One of the two temples on top of the Templo Mayor, the one painted red, was his.

I start with “pa” and rhyme with “ganga.”

My stage name includes the name of an angel.

He met Moctezuma in Tenochtitlan.
La Malinche was his interpreter.
questions.fun_fact: The chronicler Bernal Díaz del Castillo wrote down the owner, the color, and the strengths of each of those first horses.

questions.description: A question for anyone who thinks “a long time ago” and “a really, really long time ago” mean the same thing.
questions.question: You're in the Zócalo, where the heart of Tenochtitlan once stood. About how long ago did the Spanish conquer it?
hints: Your great-grandparents didn't see it, and neither did their grandparents.
It happened about 30 years after Columbus reached America.
It was in 1521.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021, Mexico marked 500 years since the fall of Tenochtitlan, and a huge model of the Templo Mayor was built in the Zócalo.

questions.question: Take a close look at this photo. What is it?
hints: In Mexico, people eat it with almost every meal.
It gets heated up on the comal.
Tacos are made with it.
questions.fun_fact: The Mexica called the tortilla “tlaxcalli” and ate it with almost everything, just like today.

hints: It isn't worn on the feet or the chest.
It's worn on the legs, but it isn't long.
Think of pants with most of the legs cut off.
questions.fun_fact: In the first soccer games of the 19th century, many players wore long pants or knee-length knickerbockers, and even a cap.

Above it, on top of a hill, stands a fortress.
Next to it are prehistoric caves that are a World Heritage Site together with those of Mitla.
questions.fun_fact: Its ball court is the largest in Oaxaca and one of the biggest in all of Mesoamerica.

questions.question: Look at the photo: in this diving event, where Mexico has won Olympic medals, two divers jump together. What do they have to do?
questions.answer: Move the same way at the same time
hints: Some judges don't watch each diver alone, but the pair as a whole.
It's the same idea as in artistic swimming or a group dance routine.
They have to look as if one were the other's reflection in a mirror.

She was one of the great poets of her time and loved studying and collecting books.
Her name starts with “Sor,” the Spanish title for a religious sister.

It gives heat and light.
The hair on the tlacuache's tail got burned off.

You say it right before you leave.

I cheer for my team from the stands.
